name: Japanese street fashion

image.caption: Japanese Street Fashion in the Kowloon Walled City (6816387287)

lead: Japanese street fashion is the collection of youth styles that grew from Tokyo districts such as Harajuku and Shibuya, including Lolita, gyaru, visual kei, decora and later techwear and genderless looks.
People adopt it to stand out and express personality, using layered clothing, hair, accessories and makeup to change their overall presentation.

paras: Followers assemble outfits from the style's signature pieces, from Victorian-inspired dresses in Lolita to tanned skin, teased hair and circle lenses in gyaru. Many follow magazines and, today, social media for ideas; some brands such as Uniqlo and GU supply simpler basics [1].

The main discussed risks are social rather than physical: cultural appropriation debates and criticism of body-image messaging in some gyaru media [3]. Makeup, lenses and bleaching carry ordinary product risks.

angle.text: Adopting a street style gives a ready-made visual system for outfits, hair and makeup, a direct way to change how a person appears.

lead: Japanese street fashion refers to clothing styles that grew from urban youth subcultures in Tokyo, centred on Harajuku and Shibuya, mixing local and international influences [1]. Well-known styles include Lolita, gyaru, visual kei, decora kei and amekaji [1].

It helps people look different by changing the whole presentation: clothing silhouettes, hair, makeup and accessories. The photographer Shoichi Aoki chronicled the scene from 1997 in the magazine FRUiTS [1]. Reference works note a shift from print magazines to Instagram and TikTok in the 2020s [2].
infobox: Lolita, gyaru, visual kei, decora, amekaji [1]

paras: Street-oriented brands existed in the 1950s, and youth culture in the 1960s and 1970s around Harajuku drove new looks; consumerism in the 1980s boom continued into the 1990s [1]. Post-war occupation brought American casual wear such as jeans and T-shirts [3]. The Takenokozoku dance groups of the late 1970s and early 1980s wore bright baggy clothes in Harajuku [3].

Lolita uses knee-length skirts, petticoats and Victorian or Rococo detail, with Gothic, Sweet and Classic sub-styles. Gyaru emphasises glamour and has sub-branches such as ganguro, popular in the early 1990s and peaking in the early 2000s [1][2]. Visual kei is a mid-1980s music-linked style with dramatic makeup and hair, and decora layers bright accessories [1].
Gyaru has drawn debate over cultural appropriation, unrealistic body-image messages in magazines and the sexualisation of schoolgirl styles [2].

timeline.event: Allied occupation introduces Western casual wear [3].
